topic: The Role of Markets and Money
subject: economics

items.title: Perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description
items.claim: Perfect competition (many small firms, homogeneous products, free entry, perfect information) is taught as a foundational market structure. Which is most accurate?

options.text: Most real markets fit the model closely
Real-world markets rarely satisfy the assumptions; agriculture, currency trading and some commodity markets come closer than most. The model is useful as a normative benchmark, not as descriptive
Perfect competition is identical to monopoly
No real-world market resembles it at all

items.reveal:
Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin 1933) and game-theoretic oligopoly models (Cournot 1838, Bertrand 1883, Stackelberg 1934) capture more of the realistic market structures.

Key deviations: most product markets have differentiated products; information is imperfect (Akerlof's 'lemons' 1970); entry has costs; small numbers of dominant firms common. The 'IO revolution' from the 1970s onwards (Tirole's textbook, 1988) built strategic-interaction-based frameworks.
items.why: The perfect competition model serves as a welfare benchmark in policy analysis. Treating it as a description of how markets work misses what most of industrial economics has been building toward.

items.title: Network effects can produce winner-take-all markets
items.claim: A product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join (telephone, social networks, payment platforms). What does this often produce?

options.text: Strong tendencies to concentration: 'winner-take-all' or 'winner-take-most' markets, often with one or two dominant firms; antitrust intervention becomes harder because consumer prices may be low while market power is high

items.reveal:
Direct network effects: more users → more value (Facebook, WhatsApp). Indirect (cross-side): more buyers attract more sellers and vice versa (Uber, marketplaces).

W. Brian Arthur's 1989 paper on increasing returns formalised the dynamics. Modern antitrust debate (Lina Khan's 2017 'Amazon's Antitrust Paradox') argues consumer-welfare frameworks miss platform power. EU Digital Markets Act (2022) and US recent FTC actions reflect this view.
items.why: Digital markets often don't fit the perfectly-competitive framework of textbook microeconomics. Regulators have had to develop new approaches as a result.

items.title: Framing changes choices on identical outcomes
items.claim: Kahneman and Tversky's classic 'Asian disease' problem: identical mortality outcomes framed differently (lives saved vs lives lost) produce systematically different preferences. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Preferences are reference-dependent and influenced by framing: gains and losses are evaluated relative to a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily (loss aversion)

items.reveal:
Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 Science paper presented the Asian disease problem. The same outcomes framed positively (lives saved) vs negatively (lives lost) reversed majority preferences between sure and probabilistic options.

The finding contradicts expected utility theory's invariance axiom. Replications include consumer choice, medical decisions and policy framing. Nudge policy uses this finding by setting defaults (organ donation opt-out vs opt-in) and framing communications.
items.why: If preferences depend on framing, then the framer is a significant agent in any choice architecture. Standard economics' assumed invariance underestimates this.
